content:
Quick answer: There is no single best shoe for every woman with plantar fasciitis. NHS advice is to choose cushioned heels and good arch support, and to avoid high heels, tight pointed shoes, flip-flops and backless slippers. Check comfort and fit in person where possible. Shoes can be part of self-care, but persistent or worsening heel pain needs advice.

This guide is a shopping checklist, not a product ranking. We have not tested or compared named shoes, and we cannot promise a recovery time or that a particular pair will treat your pain. Women's footwear ranges vary in width, shape and support. Choose for your own feet and the activities you need to do, rather than a label saying "orthopaedic" or "best for plantar fasciitis".

Start with the heel pain, not the shoe label

Plantar fasciitis causes pain under the foot around the heel and arch. Pain may be worse on the first steps after resting and after prolonged standing or walking. However, not all heel pain is plantar fasciitis. The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital's heel-pain guide describes other possible causes, including a heel-bone stress fracture and thinning of the heel's fat pad. Do not use a footwear purchase as a diagnosis.

If arthritis also affects your feet, or you already use prescribed insoles, ask a podiatrist or your treating team how footwear should fit your particular needs. A general heel-pain guide cannot assess a swollen joint, a change in foot shape or your walking pattern.

A practical shoe-fitting checklist

The NHS's starting points are cushioned heels and good arch support. Use the following questions to compare pairs in the shop or at home within the retailer's return conditions. These are practical fit checks, not a validated medical score.

  • Heel cushioning: Does the heel feel comfortably cushioned when you walk, rather than hard or worn down?
  • Arch support: Is there comfortable support under the arch without a painful ridge pressing into it?
  • Toe space and width: Can your toes sit comfortably without being squeezed by a pointed front or a narrow upper?
  • Secure fit: Can you fasten the shoe comfortably and walk without gripping with your toes to keep it on?
  • Your usual insole: If you use one, bring it to the fitting. Does it sit properly without making the shoe tight or lifting your heel out?
  • Your real activity: Try the pair for the setting you need: a work shift, ordinary walking or home. Check workplace safety requirements too.
  • Returns: Ask whether you can try the shoes indoors and return them if they are uncomfortable. Check the actual retailer's terms.

You do not need to buy the most expensive pair to follow these checks. This page does not quote current UK prices or stock because we have not verified individual products. Price, a thick-looking sole or a comfort claim alone does not establish suitability.

Trainers, work shoes, sandals and shoes for home

Everyday trainers and walking shoes

The Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital gives running trainers as an example of footwear with extra cushioning and arch support. That does not make every trainer suitable: compare the actual fit and comfort of the pair. Avoid continuing with shoes that are visibly worn or uncomfortable just because the model once felt supportive.

Work shoes

If your work requires particular footwear, take that requirement to a footwear fitter, podiatrist or occupational-health team. Look for a secure fit and the support described above within those rules. Shoes do not remove the strain of prolonged standing: NHS advice includes avoiding long periods of standing or walking while symptoms are troublesome. Discuss practical changes to your working day if needed.

Sandals and slippers

The NHS specifically advises against flip-flops and backless slippers. A sandal marketed for comfort is not automatically suitable. Check support, fit and how securely it stays on. At home, consider how you will follow the NHS advice to avoid walking barefoot on hard surfaces, rather than only thinking about your outdoor shoes.

Occasion shoes

The NHS advises against high heels and tight pointed shoes. If a dress code makes this difficult, consider a different style that leaves room for your toes and gives comfortable cushioning and support. Do not push through worsening pain to keep wearing a particular pair.

Do insoles or heel pads help?

The NHS includes insoles and heel pads among self-care options. A pharmacist can advise about these and whether you should see a GP. A podiatrist can recommend footwear and insoles for your needs if symptoms persist. Bring the shoes you actually wear to that conversation.

Do not assume you need custom-made orthotics before you have had advice, or stack several inserts into a shoe that then becomes tight. If you already have a prescribed device, ask the clinician who supplied it about fit and any new discomfort. There is no single insole recommendation on this page that is right for everyone.

Shoes are only one part of self-care

The NHS plantar-fasciitis page also recommends resting and raising the foot when possible, regular gentle stretches for the sole and heel, and considering activities that do not put pressure on the feet, such as swimming. Its page explains cold-pack use and other options. A pharmacist can help with pain-relief choices, particularly if you already take arthritis medicines.

For illustrated exercise instructions, use the Royal National Orthopaedic Hospital guide or the RDaSH NHS heel-pain guide. If you are unsure an exercise is appropriate, or it makes symptoms worse, seek advice rather than forcing it.

It may help to note what you wore, roughly how long you stood or walked, and what happened to pain afterwards. The symptom and flare tracker can organise those notes for an appointment. It is not a diagnostic test or a reason to delay care.

When should heel pain be checked?

Do not wait for a new pair of shoes to work if you need medical advice. The NHS advises seeing a GP if:

  • the pain is severe or stops normal activities;
  • it is getting worse or keeps returning;
  • it has not improved after two weeks of self-care;
  • you have tingling or loss of feeling in the foot; or
  • you have diabetes and foot pain, because foot problems can be more serious.

A physiotherapist or podiatrist may help if symptoms do not settle. Local access and NHS availability vary; the NHS page explains that MSK self-referral is possible in many areas. For an injury or urgent concern, seek appropriate urgent advice rather than relying on this checklist.

Questions to take to a fitting or appointment

  • Does my pain need an assessment before I buy anything?
  • What support and fit should I look for with my foot shape and arthritis?
  • Will my existing insole fit this shoe correctly?
  • What can I change about standing, walking or work while symptoms settle?
  • When should I come back if things are not improving?

For a broader arthritis footwear discussion, read our walking-shoes guide. It is a separate topic, not proof that a shoe treats plantar fasciitis. The most useful next step is a comfortable fit, a sensible self-care plan and timely advice when symptoms need checking.

key_takeaways: Choose comfortable heel cushioning, arch support and a fit that does not squeeze your toes.
Bring any existing insoles to the fitting and check the actual retailer return terms.
New shoes do not replace an assessment: see a GP for severe, worsening or recurrent pain, or pain not improving after two weeks of self-care.
